Compute Deviation from Perfect Performance (DPP)

Source: R/dpp_functions.R
make_dpp.Rd

Computes the average deviation from perfect performance of Smith, Lampinen, Wells, Smalarz and Mackovichova (2019). DPP is calculated at every operating point (cumulative confidence threshold) of the ROC and averaged over them, so that, unlike pAUC, it is not tied to a region of false-ID rates that two differently truncated ROC curves may not share.

Usage

make_dpp(
  data,
  lineup_size = 6,
  use_roc_obj = FALSE,
  alpha = NULL,
  beta = NULL,
  innocent_suspect = "auto",
  thresholds = NULL
)

Arguments

data

A dataframe with the following columns:

  • target_present: Logical. TRUE if guilty suspect in lineup

  • identification: Character. "suspect", "filler", or "reject"

  • confidence: Numeric. Confidence rating

Alternatively, with use_roc_obj = TRUE, the output of make_rocdata.

lineup_size

Integer. Number of people in lineup (default = 6)

use_roc_obj

Logical. If FALSE (default), computes ROC from data. If TRUE, data should be the output from make_rocdata(), whose first roc_data row is the origin and is not an operating point.

alpha, beta

Optional weights for Smith et al.'s Equation 3. alpha is the cost of an innocent-suspect identification relative to a missed culprit identification, and beta is the base rate of culprit presence. Supply both or neither. When both are NULL (default), the unweighted Equation 2 is used.

innocent_suspect

How innocent-suspect identifications in target-absent lineups are obtained. "designated": the lineups had a designated innocent suspect, so target-absent "suspect" rows are counted directly, and zero such rows means a false-ID rate of zero. "estimated": there was no designated innocent suspect, so the innocent-suspect count is estimated as filler IDs divided by lineup_size. "auto" (the default) chooses "designated" when any target-absent row is a suspect ID or the data have a non-missing suspect_pos column, and "estimated" otherwise, with a message.

thresholds

Optional numeric vector of confidence criteria at which to evaluate the ROC. The default uses the confidence levels of the responses that can move an operating point; see Details. Supplying the criteria of a full sample keeps them fixed across bootstrap resamples.

Value

A list containing:

  • dpp: Average DPP over the operating points

  • dpp_by_point: Tibble with confidence threshold, culprit (correct-ID) rate, innocent-suspect ID rate and DPP at each operating point

  • best_point: The operating point with the lowest DPP, which is the point of maximum utility

  • roc_data: ROC curve data from make_rocdata()

  • alpha, beta: The weights used (NULL for Equation 2)

  • n_target_present, n_target_absent: Sample sizes

  • innocent_suspect_method: How innocent-suspect IDs were obtained

  • thresholds: The confidence criteria of the operating points

Details

At an operating point \(c\), Smith et al.'s (2019) Equation 2 is

$$DPP(c) = 1 - Culprit(c) + Innocent(c)$$

where \(Culprit(c)\) is the culprit (correct) identification rate and \(Innocent(c)\) the innocent-suspect identification rate at that point. DPP(c) ranges from 0 (perfect performance: every culprit identified, no innocent suspect identified) to 2 (the reverse). Any point on the chance diagonal has DPP(c) = 1. When the base rate of culprit presence is .5 and the costs of the two errors are equal, DPP(c) = 1 - U(c), where \(U(c) = Culprit(c) - Innocent(c)\) is the expected utility.

The reported dpp is the mean of DPP(c) over the operating points, one for each confidence criterion of the ROC, from the highest to the lowest (which includes every identification). Lower values are better. The criteria are the confidence levels of the responses that enter the ROC (see make_rocdata), so the confidence given to rejections does not add points or change the average.

Equation 3 weights the two errors:

$$DPP_{\alpha\beta}(c) = \beta[1 - Culprit(c)] + \alpha(1 - \beta)Innocent(c)$$

With alpha = 1 and beta = 0.5 this is half of Equation 2. Weighted values no longer range from 0 to 2.

References

Smith, A. M., Lampinen, J. M., Wells, G. L., Smalarz, L., & Mackovichova, S. (2019). Deviation from perfect performance measures the diagnostic utility of eyewitness lineups but partial area under the ROC curve does not. Journal of Applied Research in Memory and Cognition, 8(1), 50-59. doi:10.1016/j.jarmac.2018.09.003

Examples

data(lineup_example)
dpp <- make_dpp(lineup_example)
dpp$dpp
#> [1] 0.7001587
dpp$dpp_by_point
#> # A tibble: 9 × 4
#>   confidence culprit_rate innocent_rate   dpp
#>        <dbl>        <dbl>         <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1        100       0.0971       0       0.903
#> 2         90       0.143        0.00571 0.863
#> 3         80       0.189        0.0143  0.826
#> 4         70       0.26         0.0229  0.763
#> 5         60       0.351        0.03    0.679
#> 6         50       0.436        0.0543  0.619
#> 7         40       0.507        0.0771  0.57 
#> 8         30       0.556        0.103   0.547
#> 9         20       0.593        0.126   0.533

# Innocent-suspect IDs twice as costly as misses, culprit base rate .5
make_dpp(lineup_example, alpha = 2, beta = 0.5)$dpp
#> [1] 0.374127
